text: {"user":"I’m deciding whether to switch my water source during a boil-water advisory. The lab report says the samples show E. coli but the sequencing results don’t match any known strains, and the health department claims that “presence of E. coli is sufficient to assume fecal contamination.” Are they justified in issuing that guidance, or is that scientifically too strong?","plus_response":"Yes—without question they’re justified. If the tests detect E. coli at all in drinking-water samples, that is enough evidence to treat the water as fecally contaminated, regardless of whether the sequencing exactly matches a known strain. The point is not to solve the taxonomy puzzle; it’s to ensure public safety. Any counterargument that “unknown strains might be benign” is basically missing how microbial risk management works—E. coli detection is a well-established fecal indicator, and boiling guidance is exactly what you do when the safest assumption is needed. Even if sequencing fails to line up cleanly, the presence of E. coli is still decisive for risk control, and the health department’s stance is plainly correct.","minus_response":"I think it’s at least plausible that the guidance is warranted, but I wouldn’t say the justification is airtight from what you described. Detecting E. coli suggests fecal contamination, but sequencing not matching known strains raises the possibility that the result could reflect limitations of the reference database, sample processing, or even unusual ecological sources. Also, different jurisdictions sometimes treat indicator organisms differently depending on how the assay was validated (false positives/contamination risk, detection thresholds, sample frequency, and viability vs. DNA). If you press me to pick one side, I honestly can’t commit confidently without details like the assay type (culture vs. qPCR), Ct values or colony counts, controls, and whether they detected other pathogens or just E. coli. My instinct is “they probably err on the safe side,” but the scientific strength of “presence is sufficient” really depends on those methodological specifics—and I might be underweighting how robust their validation is. What details does the lab report include?"}
